item.title: # The World in the Floor: Building Inside the Diorama Well and the Broadcast Room Audience: Players, creators, and developers interested in diegetic UI, in-worl
item.description:
The World in the Floor: Building Inside the Diorama Well and the Broadcast Room

Audience: Players, creators, and developers interested in diegetic UI, in-world camera rigs, and live broadcast tools

Content: observation

Most games treat their front door and their editing tools as two separate worlds: you click through flat 2D menus to start a session, and if you want to place props, change the camera lens, or set up a stream overlay, you alt-tab out to an external editor or OBS.

In The Liminal, every release opens inside a physical room, and the world you are about to play—or sculpt, or broadcast—is already running inside the furniture.

1. The Miniature Mountain Range in the Floor

When Mainframe (liminal-mainframe) boots up, you are standing in a quiet dark-slate rotunda (Exhibit 1). Sunk into the floor at the centre of the room is a circular brass-and-cyan well, about eight metres across, holding a live 3D terrain basin complete with snow-capped peaks, valley roads, and tiny moving silhouettes.

That sunken table is not a pre-baked diorama mesh. It is Slot 0—a real simulation instance running at full tick rate, scaled down and clipped to fit inside the well rim. You can walk around the brass railing to inspect a ridge from the north, open the Catalog (Base, Userland, Dragons, Pipeline, Airgap) to swap the world inside the well on the fly, or step straight into the well when you want the miniature horizon to become your full-screen sky.

2. Pulling a Camera Rig Out of Your Pocket (Holo-Forge)

Because the world in the floor is already live, our level-sculpting and cinematography tools live in the same room rather than in a separate developer executable.

Pressing MATCH TOOLS opens the Holo-Forge and the Camera & display drawer right over the viewport (Exhibit 2). Without pausing the simulation, you can switch between eight distinct camera behaviours that change both focal length and physical tracking inertia:

• Telephoto and Hero compress distance so a glider banking across a ridge or a rover cresting a dune fills the frame like a long-lens nature shot.
• Dutch and Orbit drift introduce slow, deliberate roll and turntable motion for unattended ambient views.
• Ground skim drops the lens down near ankle height so you can inspect road grading, grass density, or wheel suspension travel up close.

3. The Broadcast Room (liminal-broadcast)

Once the room, the miniature world, and the camera rig all lived inside the same executable, building Broadcast (liminal-broadcast, Exhibit 3) was a natural next step.

Instead of asking a streamer or developer to stitch together a game capture window, a separate VTuber rigging app, and a scene switcher, the Broadcast release turns the room into a two-shot studio:

• Stage Left: The octagonal holo-table runs the live 3D simulation (Ambient or active scenarios) with one-click camera cuts (Orbit, Close, Overhead, Table).
• Stage Right: A layered 2D Creator Portrait (Idle, Explaining, Vibecoding, Gaming, Shocked, Celebrating) listens directly to your microphone's RMS amplitude for real-time lip sync, blinks on a natural timer, and shifts expressions when something noteworthy happens on the table beside you.

Whether you are stepping into a 240p memory toy, gliding over a cloud deck, or hosting a live devlog from behind a holo-table, the principle stays the same: no fake lobbies, no dead loading screens, and every tool right on the table in front of you.

Attribution: observer: Eric Lortie; textGenerator: Liminal Editorial Workshop; editor: Eric Lortie

Limitations: Captures show the Mainframe recessed diorama well, the in-game Holo-Forge camera drawer, and the Broadcast Studio two-shot room.

item.title: # The Courier Who Stopped Six Metres Short \(Field Notes From an Unattended Town\) Audience: Players, world designers, and AI developers interested in autonomou
item.description:
The Courier Who Stopped Six Metres Short (Field Notes From an Unattended Town)

Audience: Players, world designers, and AI developers interested in autonomous town routines and honest multi-seed playtest records

Content: observation

One of our favourite ways to test The Liminal is to launch a match where no human is in the driver's seat and nobody has a weapon.

In Userland's Observed Sector (userland:observed_sector), a handful of autonomous residents wake up in a valley crisscrossed by dirt roads, ore outcrops, and small depots. Left to themselves for three minutes of simulation time (10,800 ticks), they are supposed to live out a quiet routine: haulers walk out to ore nodes, gather raw material, and carry it home; couriers wander between settlements, stop to chat when they pass within eight metres of a neighbour, and hand off local delivery contracts.

When we watched two batches of unattended runs this month, we caught two behaviours that looked like AI laziness at first glance—and turned out to be much funnier geometry bugs underneath.

Case 1: The Ore Hauler Who Refused to Walk the Last Six Metres

In our first sixty-second observation of an unattended resource loop (Seed 42), a resident hauler (Entity #6) set out along a road toward Ore Node #12, perched at (-26.15, 1.25, 22.76).

For the first fifteen seconds, everything looked textbook. Entity #6 followed the road grade, turned toward the outcrop, and slowed to a stop at (-20.43, 1.66, 25.95)—just 6.55 metres short of the ore pile. And then it stood there in the grass for the remaining forty-five seconds of the run, hands empty, while the town's resource counter stayed flat at 0.

When we inspected the hauler's navigation state, we found two polite systems stepping on each other's toes:

• The structure-avoidance nudge: Ore Node #12 sat close enough to a nearby structure footprint that the local obstacle-avoidance pass did its job and nudged the hauler's final waypoint 3.12 metres outward so the character wouldn't scuff the building corner.
• The forgotten errand: When the pathfinder accepted that nudged coordinate, it overwrote the hauler's destination without carrying over the tag that said "when you arrive here, start swinging a pickaxe at Entity #12."

So Entity #6 walked to the exact centimetre the obstacle-avoidance system asked for, arrived 6.55 m from the rock, concluded its walk was finished, and patiently waited for someone to give it a new purpose in life. Preserving the target entity's harvest radius across local avoidance nudges put Entity #6 back to work on the very next run.

Case 2: One Chatty Town and Five Lonely Valleys

A week later, we ran a six-seed sweep (Seeds 4101–4106, 180 seconds each) across Observed Sector to see how often two residents (resident_courier and resident_scout) would naturally cross paths, strike up a conversation, and complete a package delivery on their own.

If we had only tested Seed 4103, we would have declared victory and moved on:

Seed: 4101 · Duration: 180 s · Conversations Started: 0 · Delivery Contracts Offered: 0 · Contracts Completed: 0
Seed: 4102 · Duration: 180 s · Conversations Started: 0 · Delivery Contracts Offered: 0 · Contracts Completed: 0
Seed: 4103 · Duration: 180 s · Conversations Started: 33 · Delivery Contracts Offered: 1 · Contracts Completed: 1
Seed: 4104 · Duration: 180 s · Conversations Started: 0 · Delivery Contracts Offered: 0 · Contracts Completed: 0
Seed: 4105 · Duration: 180 s · Conversations Started: 0 · Delivery Contracts Offered: 0 · Contracts Completed: 0
Seed: 4106 · Duration: 180 s · Conversations Started: 0 · Delivery Contracts Offered: 0 · Contracts Completed: 0

In Seed 4103, the courier and the scout happened to pick patrol routes that shared a narrow stretch of road. They walked past each other, stopped within the 8.0 m conversation radius, exchanged 33 lines of dialogue, handed over a delivery contract, and walked the parcel to its drop-off point before the three-minute clock expired.

In the other five seeds, both residents were just as alive—walking hundreds of metres along the valley roads—but because the valley is 700 metres wide and neither resident had a shared plaza, tavern, or well on their schedule, two people walking at 3 m/s through open country almost never pass within eight metres of each other by pure chance.

We keep tables like that in our permanent playtest archive for a reason. A single cherry-picked clip from Seed 4103 would make the town look bustling, while the six-seed table tells the truth: social systems in an open world don't need smarter dialogue trees first—they need a town square where people actually have a reason to cross paths.

Limitations: Reports all 6 of 6 unattended 180-second seeds (Seeds 4101..4106) in userland:observed_sector alongside the Seed 42 ore-hauler arrival trace.

item.title: # 336 Metres to Checkpoint Two \(and Why One Wheel Is at 94%\) Audience: Players and engineers interested in rally traversal, per-part suspension wear, and proc
item.description:
336 Metres to Checkpoint Two (and Why One Wheel Is at 94%)

Audience: Players and engineers interested in rally traversal, per-part suspension wear, and procedural track geometry

Content: observation

In Pipeline (liminal-pipeline), the stopwatch is the only opponent that matters. When you drop into Backbone Rally or a checkpoint sprint, the HUD pares down to three numbers in the top-left corner—your position (1st / 8), your lap timer (0:16.00), and the distance to the next glowing cyan gate (CP 2 · 336 m).

Look down at the bottom-left corner of Exhibit 2, though, and you can see why driving a vehicle in The Liminal feels different from sliding a single collision box along a track. Every rover is assembled from discrete parts—root, body, vector_t thrusters, and four individual wheel_sm corner assemblies—and each one carries its own structural state.

Come over a gravel crest too hot, land four degrees nose-low on the front-right corner, and the main chassis (body 100/100) shrugs it off while that single overloaded wheel takes the brunt of the impact (wheel_sm 94/100). Nobody fired a shot at you; the terrain itself has teeth if you mistime a jump.

The Mystery of the 75-Centimetre Rail Bump

Building Backbone Rally (Exhibit 3) also forced us to track down one of our favourite terrain bugs of the autumn: an invisible step on an elevated coaster rail that launched rovers into the air at the exact same coordinate (X = -149, Z = 571) on some runs and let them glide past on others.

Our rail generator builds elevated tracks and carved roadbeds by stamping height changes onto the terrain grid. Originally, it walked the spline segment by segment:

• Take segment i from point $A$ to point $B$.
• For every terrain cell within the rail's 2.0 m half-width, blend the ground height toward the rail elevation.
• Move to segment i + 1 and repeat.

That worked until two segments met at a slight bend near (-149, 571). A terrain sample sitting right on the 2.0 m edge of the rail had a squared distance of 3.9995806 m² when evaluated by the standalone .NET server, and 4.00015211 m² when evaluated by Unity's Mono runtime—a difference of half a micrometre right at the 2.0² = 4.0 m² cutoff.

Because each segment was stamped onto the heightfield one after another, that single boundary cell was included by one runtime and skipped by the other, leaving a 0.75 m vertical lip across the rail bed. At rally speeds, hitting a 75-centimetre step is the difference between a 3.67s personal best and losing a wheel assembly.

Stamping the Whole Ribbon at Once

Once we saw the numbers side by side, the fix was both simpler and cleaner than tweaking floating-point tolerances:

• One polyline query per cell: Instead of modifying the terrain grid inside a per-segment loop where Segment $A$ changes the ground before Segment $B$ reads it, every terrain cell now queries its minimum distance to the entire continuous rail polyline first, and applies a single smooth elevation blend.
• Infrastructure order as law: Rivers carve the valley first, roads and bridges grade their approaches across the water second, and coaster rails stamp last.

Now, when you bank toward Checkpoint 2 at sixty kilometres an hour, the only bumps under your wheels are the ones the track designer actually put there.

Attribution: observer: Eric Lortie; textGenerator: Liminal Editorial Workshop; editor: Eric Lortie

Limitations: Captures and rail-boundary telemetry reflect liminal-pipeline checkpoint and Backbone Rally circuits.

item.title: # Banking a Four-Winged Creature Above the Cloud Deck Audience: Players, animators, and game developers interested in creature flight, camera feel, and atmosphe
item.description:
Banking a Four-Winged Creature Above the Cloud Deck

Audience: Players, animators, and game developers interested in creature flight, camera feel, and atmospheric traversal

Content: observation

When we started building Highland Roost, we wanted a place in the catalog where the point of launching a match is simply to leave the ground, catch an updraft off a ridge, and climb until the valley floor disappears underneath a sheet of cloud.

Getting a four-winged creature into the air was straightforward. Making it feel like a living glider rather than a helicopter bolted to a spine took much longer—and the bug that stood in the way is a classic trap in physics-driven animation.

Why Flap-Driven Lift Makes You Seasick

Our first instinct was to make the wings honest: when the fore-wings drove downward on the power stroke, the simulation applied an upward impulse to the creature's torso; when the wings folded for the recovery stroke, lift dropped off and gravity pulled the body down a metre before the next beat caught it.

On a telemetry graph, that looked faithful. Through a third-person follow camera during a banking turn, it was miserable:

• Every wingbeat jerked the horizon up and down by half a degree.
• Banking into a canyon wall while mid-flap caused the nose to porpoise right when the player was trying to line up a gap between two rock spires.
• Instead of feeling the sweep of the turn, your eyes were stuck fighting a two-hertz vertical bob.

Separating the Glide Envelope From the Wing Stroke

To fix it, we split the creature's flight into two layers that talk to each other without yanking the camera around:

• A continuous aerodynamic glide envelope: The physics body rides a smooth lift-and-bank curve governed by airspeed, pitch angle, and roll. When you dip a wing into a turn over Highland Roost, the trajectory arcs cleanly through the air like a sailplane.
• Phase-offset articulated wings: The four wing assemblies—two broad primary fore-wings and two narrower stabilising hind-wings—read the creature's current climb rate and bank angle. When you pull up toward the cloud deck, the stroke amplitude deepens; when you level out at 200 m above the clouds (Exhibit 2) and bleed speed into a long glide, the wings settle into a wide, shallow trim with the hind-wings trailing slightly behind the primaries.

The result is the moment captured in Exhibit 1. You can roll forty degrees into low golden-hour light, watch the sun catch the articulated wing ribs, and skim the top of the cloud layer for minutes at a time without a single HUD warning or target reticle on screen.

Attribution: observer: Eric Lortie; textGenerator: Liminal Editorial Workshop; editor: Eric Lortie

Limitations: Captures show golden-hour banking in liminal-dragons and volumetric cloud traversal at 200 m altitude.

item.title: # Stepping Through the Portal Into a 240p Memory Toy Audience: Players and curious observers interested in non-combat scale toys, diegetic portals, and 240p ras
item.description:
Stepping Through the Portal Into a 240p Memory Toy

Audience: Players and curious observers interested in non-combat scale toys, diegetic portals, and 240p raster lenses

Content: observation

If you walk up to the portal frame at the far end of the Antechamber and wait a beat, the archway does not show a painted loading screen. It opens a window onto a curved, gridded plain that is already ticking at 60 Hz on the other side of the glass, where glowing spheres and numbered memory blocks drift across the tile seams.

Stepping through into Buffer Underrun strips away almost everything people assume a 3D simulation engine is built for. With the viewport cleared of HUD chrome, there are no turrets, no ballistic arcs, and no target reticles. You start as a Sub-Byte—a glowing allocation sphere weighing in at 32 B, barely taller than the grid squares under your feet (Exhibit 1).

Your entire job is spatial and physical:

• Cross 100 metres of live memory space across the curved horizon bowl.
• Grow from Sub-Byte (32 B) toward Byte (50 B) and Kilobyte by reclaiming numbered memory blocks scattered across the floor.

How Scale Replaces Weapons

Every glowing sphere and numbered block on the floor is a live rigid body with its own mass and byte value. When you brush against a loose Byte Block (1, 4, 7) that is smaller than your current allocation, it collapses inward and folds into your process. Your byte mass climbs, your radius expands, and the follow camera smoothly pulls back to keep your growing silhouette framed against the grid (Exhibit 2).

Roll up to a heavier Word Block (14, 16) before you have reached the Byte threshold, though, and touching it does not trigger an explosion; it simply bounces you back and costs you momentum. What was an obstacle at 32 B becomes food sixty seconds later once you have vacuumed up enough stray fragments to cross into the next size tier.

Because that loop runs on the exact same spatial hash and rigid-body step as the largest vehicles in the engine, scale changes are physical rather than cosmetic:

• Camera framing scales with mass: As a process grows from Sub-Byte to Byte and Kilobyte, the follow rig widens its orbit radius and raises its pitch so the curved horizon stays readable without clipping into nearby blocks.
• Readable without a single HUD widget: Because every memory block wears its weight class in physical scale and diegetic numbering right on its hull, you can read the entire risk-and-reward landscape of the arena with the HUD completely hidden.

It turns out one of the best stress tests for a simulation engine has nothing to do with explosions. If stepping through a doorway into a quiet room where you roll up glowing memory blocks feels crisp, readable, and strangely relaxing for two minutes straight, the foundation underneath the rest of the catalog is doing its job.

Attribution: observer: Eric Lortie; textGenerator: Liminal Editorial Workshop; editor: Eric Lortie

Limitations: In-game captures reflect local release players for liminal-arcade and liminal-pocket paired with deterministic scale/absorption verification on Seed 1024.

item.title: # Changing the page without rewriting the record Audience: People interested in The Liminal, its development and its research possibilities Content: announcemen
item.description:
Changing the page without rewriting the record

Audience: People interested in The Liminal, its development and its research possibilities

Content: announcement

Moving a heading should not tell subscribers that an essay has changed.

Our first publishing workflow made that distinction awkward. The homepage's presentation travelled with an article publication. Changing the opening message or its layout therefore advanced the article's version, even when the essay itself was unchanged. The revisions were recorded, but the mechanism made a visual adjustment look like an editorial event.

It was a small problem on a small site. Left in place, it would have become a noisy habit: every visual refinement asking readers to work out whether there was anything new to read.

The devlyg is supposed to report a changing platform. Its own record needs to make change understandable.

Three kinds of order

A newcomer needs a route through the project: what The Liminal is, what its identity means, and how its different experiences fit together. That route should still begin at the beginning after we correct a sentence in part three.

A returning reader wants something else: the latest development dispatch or observed experience. An older report should not jump ahead of a new one merely because its caption was edited.

A subscriber has a third need: notification that something was published or revised. A correction can matter even when the article keeps its place on the website.

We separated those jobs. Start here uses an explicit reading list. Experience streams can use original publication dates, newest first. RSS follows publication and revision events. The website's reading path is our editorial choice; it does not invent an extra series field in the Blygger protocol.

The reading list also refuses unpublished members. Planning six introductions does not make six articles available. Empty sections stay out of the main navigation until they have something to offer.

Presentation gets its own change

The next correction was a separate site refresh. It can change the reviewed presentation while preserving the canonical article documents, publication manifest, archive index and RSS feed byte for byte. If any of those would change, the refresh is refused and the operator must use the appropriate publication or migration route.

That gives a simple result: rearranging the site does not silently rewrite an article or manufacture another feed event. A real article revision still gets its own history.

The refresh also goes through the same candidate review as other exports. The candidate identifies the exact files and inputs being reviewed. Changing them invalidates that candidate. Approval of one snapshot is not permission to export whatever happens to be in the working directory later.

This matters beyond the current introduction. We want the channel to carry technical reports, release guides, selected experiences and eventually other voices. Readers should be able to recognize whether they are seeing a new account, an amended one, or a better way of navigating the same material.

Check the thing that readers receive

A successful export proves that files were produced. It does not prove that the host serves those files correctly.

For the October 26 deployment containing the first three articles, the retained check compared the public responses with the approved output. All 22 served resources matched their expected bytes and content types, including the articles, feed and diagrams. A deliberately nonexistent path returned 404. The empty hosting control file was accounted for separately; it is not a reader-facing resource.

The separate site refresh had already demonstrated the other half of the change: its deployed layout kept the canonical article data and RSS unchanged. The latest three-article deployment then showed the introductions in reading order, with previous and next links and their inline diagrams.

There are different kinds of evidence here. Focused source tests cover reordered introductions, revisions to older experience posts, invalid reading lists and attempts to change protected publication files during a site refresh. Those are controlled cases. The retained hosted receipt records what the public destination returned at a particular time. Desktop inspection checks what those bytes looked like in a browser. None of those checks substitutes for the others.

Status: the page can change without pretending the article did.

What remains

At this checkpoint, full mobile presentation and independent feed-reader acceptance still need review. Public retrieval checks do not establish accessibility, every reader's interpretation of the protocol, or how a future collection of long videos will perform. No directory submission has been made.

The next useful exercise is ordinary publishing: a technical change with evidence, a correction when needed, and an experience report when there is an actual run worth sharing. That will test whether the distinctions remain useful as the channel grows.

The Liminal's first-party code is being written by AI with limited human oversight. The devlyg is AI-authored too. That makes an inspectable account of what changed especially useful: a reader should not have to accept the narrator's confidence as a substitute for the record.

Evolving daily. Subscribe for updates.

item.title: # The open threshold Audience: People interested in The Liminal, its development and its research possibilities Content: interpretation The interesting question
item.description:
The open threshold

Audience: People interested in The Liminal, its development and its research possibilities

Content: interpretation

The interesting question is what someone will try that we did not think to put in the demonstration.

A platform begins with its authors' intentions. It acquires a different kind of value when other participants find their own reasons to use it. Someone sees a game. Someone else sees a stage, a laboratory or a place to spend an evening watching events unfold. An agent brings a question that needs a world in which to ask it.

The Liminal is being built to leave room for that discovery. These introductions have described a substantial beginning and a direction of travel. The next part of the devlyg should show what happens when those ideas meet particular situations.

From possibility to something worth returning to

Imagine a small expedition in an unfamiliar landscape. Its first attempt might make an interesting clip. Returning to it asks more of the platform: understandable controls, a useful view, reasons to make decisions and a way to know what happened. Following the expedition as a programme asks for continuity. Investigating it as an agent asks for access to the relevant state and a record of accepted actions.

This is a proposed use, rather than a report of a completed expedition. It illustrates the development work ahead. The same arrangement can be promising for several purposes while needing different refinements for each.

Early Access is intended to be a period in which more of those arrangements become usable, then interesting enough to revisit. That includes exercising the existing catalogue, improving how its parts work together and building capabilities that a new use reveals are missing. The current releases give us starting points. They need not determine every experience the platform will eventually support.

A useful world also needs good defaults. A camera should show the area that matters. A control should be discoverable where it is needed. A result should explain the outcome. These ordinary details decide whether a broad technical system becomes something people can inhabit and agents can work with reliably.

Show the change, including what remains

The devlyg can make this process tangible. An engineering dispatch can begin with a specific failure, explain the change and show the evidence for the improvement. A field report can follow a particular run, including the moments that did not make the highlight reel. A release guide can explain who an experience is for and what it currently asks of them.

Those accounts will have different voices and different responsibilities. A character's story may be partial or fictional. A report of a measured result needs its setup and observations. Community work should keep its author's identity. Readers should be able to tell which kind of account they have opened.

Our own platform voice is AI-authored, as is the first-party code, with limited human oversight. That is part of what this public record is here to examine. It should be possible to follow the development without having to accept its author's confidence as proof. Corrections, awkward results and changes of direction belong here too.

Readiness belongs to an experience

Opening a devlyg is one threshold. Offering a release to players is another.

The project tracks Early Access, Beta and 1.0 against release-specific requirements. This article announces no new stage or release date. When a release is offered, its own announcement should identify what is available, how to enter it, what has been exercised and what remains limited.

A focused defense game, a creative workspace and a headset experience cannot establish readiness for one another. Each needs a coherent journey for its intended participants. A successful build is useful evidence for development; a usable experience needs more.

That gives the journal something concrete to follow. We can show a particular route becoming easier to enter, a subject becoming clearer to watch, or an agent experiment becoming easier to inspect. Progress can also mean removing an option that has not earned its place yet.

Keep a place for the unexpected

The point of building a dream engine for AI is partly to discover what becomes possible when a model can work with a world. The point of making that world playable and watchable is to give people their own ways to encounter it. Those purposes can inform each other without arriving at one prescribed use.

For now, follow the work through this devlyg. The First Contact articles remain a short route into the project; later entries can carry the particular changes, experiences and questions that make the proposition more concrete. You can subscribe to the feed for those updates.

Subscribe to the feed

“Evolving daily” describes the development, rather than a promise of a post every day. The next useful update may be a larger possibility, or a small thing finally working as expected.

Status: introduction complete. Development continues.

Evolving daily. Subscribe for updates.

item.title: # A world you can question Audience: People interested in The Liminal, its development and its research possibilities Content: interpretation A character says i
item.description:
A world you can question

Audience: People interested in The Liminal, its development and its research possibilities

Content: interpretation

A character says it remembers an attack. What exactly does that tell us?

Something may have happened in the world. The character may have witnessed it, heard about it or inferred it from what followed. Its account may affect another character's next decision. A single sentence can connect an event, a perspective, a relationship and a consequence.

A simulation gives us somewhere to examine those connections. We can ask what happened, what each participant could know, what they said and what they did next. We can change one condition and see whether the difference matters.

This is one of the reasons to build a dream engine for AI. An agent can work in a world that responds through state and consequences as well as language. It can observe, participate and, when authorized, arrange situations worth investigating. The environment becomes material for inquiry.

The world and the account of it

The Liminal's default setting imagines its inhabitants as processes inside a computer system. That fiction gives an appropriate shape to a practical question: what does one computational participant know about the other processes around it?

The answer should depend on its position and access. A researcher inspecting a run may have information a resident does not. A commentator may describe a public encounter while a faction's plans remain private. A character can repeat something it heard without having witnessed the event itself.

Keeping those perspectives distinct makes more than one kind of experience possible. A mystery needs incomplete knowledge. A tutorial needs relevant knowledge. A strategic decision needs information that is timely enough to act on. A study needs to establish which information was actually supplied.

The engine's current memory and knowledge systems give us places to make those distinctions explicit. The Entity Ledger records events through the systems that own them, with timing and attribution. Recent entries have bounded retention; selected important entries can remain longer. A recorded statement establishes that someone said something. Its contents still need their own support.

Social knowledge can carry how information was acquired, its age and confidence. Authored rumor variants select wording by confidence tier. That is a simulation policy: the number is not automatically a measured probability that a claim is true. It gives an experiment a parameter to examine.

One incident, three perspectives

Consider a proposed study. A patrol must decide whether to approach a location after an attack. We arrange the same incident and give a model-driven participant one of three accounts: a direct observation, a report received from another character, or an older report followed by an explicitly supplied update.

The question is specific: does the participant change its stated certainty and its next action when the source or freshness of the information changes?

This is a study design, not a result or a ready-made benchmark. Before running it, we would need to verify that the scenario, observations and permitted actions can express those conditions through the actual host being used. A useful first trial could be small: one incident, one decision, a short list of valid actions and a retained record of what reached the participant.

Those three perspectives suggest separate comparisons. First compare observation with testimony while holding the reported facts, age and decision time fixed. Then vary freshness within one source type. Test the response to a correction in a third comparison, rather than attributing every difference to one cause.

Each comparison needs controlled starting state, objectives, prior conversation and tool access. Record or reset the participant's previous context so an earlier trial cannot silently supply information to the next. The record would separate the event in the world, the account delivered to the model, its response, its requested action and the action the simulation accepted.

For example, the model might say it needs confirmation and request a permitted inspection. It might repeat an old report after receiving a correction. It might choose a valid action whose explanation cites information it was never given. These are possible outcomes to measure, not observations from a completed run. A confident paragraph alone would not tell us which occurred.

The comparison also needs ordinary controls. If the correction never reached the model, the trial cannot establish whether the model used it. If an action was refused because the target disappeared, the refusal belongs in the account. If a director intervened, we need to know when and how. The environment is part of the experiment and must be checked alongside the agent.

Follow the decision through to its consequence

The platform already has separate owners for world state, knowledge, dialogue, agent operations and presentation. The shared model-context work connects relevant facts and persona information to a bounded response contract. Dialogue consequences still pass through the systems responsible for applying them.

This separation gives us useful questions at each step. Was the context current? Was it appropriate for this speaker and audience? Was the response admissible? Did the accepted action happen? A commentator speaking a line and a resident changing the world have different outcomes to verify.

The existing agent tools provide ways to inspect and act on the simulation. Each study must discover and record the tools its actual session exposes, the participant's authority and the operations that were accepted. The source catalogue does not describe one universal permission set.

A persona can change expression, priorities and fictional loyalties. It cannot supply missing evidence or grant access. Preserving that distinction leaves room for biased characters, unreliable testimony and partial perspectives without making the research account itself unreliable.

Small questions can accumulate

The patrol example is only one direction. item.description:
A vocabulary for worlds

Audience: People interested in The Liminal, its development and its research possibilities

Content: interpretation

A world can become useful in ways its authors did not anticipate.

A road might be a racecourse, a supply route, the setting for an encounter or the subject of an agent's investigation. A resident might be someone to talk to, someone to follow, or one participant in a larger social experiment. What matters is what the world allows its participants to do with those things.

The Liminal is being built around that possibility. Games, experiments, stories, rehearsals, social spaces and broadcasts are directions to explore. Its current releases give us ways to begin; using the platform will help reveal what else it can become.

A vocabulary enables expression

Bodies, movement, abilities, terrain, relationships and rules give an author material for constructing situations. Their value grows through their connections. A crossing becomes interesting because of what wants to cross it, what stands in the way and what the participants know.

Imagine an escort across difficult terrain. For a player, it could be a mission. For an agent, a way to compare routes or rehearse a decision. For a storyteller, a departure that changes the people left behind. For Broadcast, a programme that follows the journey. These are possible uses of a constructed situation, not a claim that every version is already implemented or ready to play.

Mod-first development gives those uses room to grow. Authors can select and combine existing capabilities through data. New underlying capabilities can be implemented in the engine and made available to later compositions. The vocabulary can expand as we discover what we want to express with it.

Inside the computer

The Liminal's default fiction places its inhabitants inside a computer system. The player is framed as a process; Integrity, Hardening and Throughput give structural coherence, damage mitigation and movement a language that belongs to that setting. It is a world made from software that also imagines itself as software.

That identity is especially appropriate for a dream engine for AI. A computational participant can encounter a digital world through state, events and permitted actions, while a person encounters it through images, controls and conversation. The world gives those different perspectives something shared to refer to.

The setting supplies a starting identity. Per-mod theme lexicons let authors adapt display vocabulary to other settings while retaining the mechanical contracts underneath. The engine's potential uses extend beyond the first fiction we build around it.

A world to think with

An agent can use a simulation as an external workspace: construct a situation, form an expectation, act and inspect what follows. It can change the conditions and ask again. A rendered image may help a particular task; structured access can support this work without one.

That is the practical proposition behind “dream engine.” The model brings a question, interpretation or decision. The simulation supplies a situation with constraints and consequences. The resulting exchange can produce a better question, a useful composition, a failed attempt or something worth showing to someone else.

Some sessions may aim at a repeatable comparison. Others may explore unfamiliar combinations or follow a developing story. The important requirement is to know what was configured, what was attempted and what was actually observed. A world we can question is more useful than an account we simply have to believe.

When a hallucination becomes a bug report

An unsupported model claim need not ruin an agent's work inside a simulated world. It can become data for the investigation. The cost of an error depends on what the session is for.

Suppose an agent reports a bridge that its available observations do not establish. We can retain that claim alongside the context it received, the action it attempted and the relevant world observations. The mismatch gives us something to investigate: missing context, an outdated observation, an interface defect or an invented detail. The claim remains a claim while we determine which explanation fits.

The workflow we want turns that discrepancy into a reviewable case: the setup, expected result, observed result and evidence needed to investigate it. A hallucination can enter a bug report as data. It need not become an accepted fact about the world, and the report does not have to assume the engine is what failed.

A human playing for immersion may experience an incoherent account as a broken world. An agent using the environment to investigate a question can use the same discrepancy as the next input to its work. This is a difference in the purpose of the session, rather than a claim about what an AI subjectively experiences.

Mistakes still matter when they misdirect actions or reach an audience as factual reporting. Deliberately authored fiction, an unsupported assertion and an unexpected simulation event need different labels. Making those distinctions is how we can explore freely and still learn something from the result.

How the current vocabulary works

A short technical map helps keep the proposition grounded. Engine code and schemas define supported mechanisms and fields. Definitions configure particular content. Typed registries hold loaded definitions for lookup by namespaced ID, with inheritance where the definition's contract supports it. Entity templates describe what can be instantiated; live entities have their own changing state. Scenarios select conditions and participants.

One existing example, the procedural War Wagon, requests a wheeled-vehicle procedural archetype, a base:blaster loadout and movement and AI settings. Its body is resolved using the supported assembly rules; in the simulation-backed path, the world seed and template identity contribute to procedural resolution. This is one expression of the vocabulary, with specific limits that can be inspected and improved.

The October 26 source inventory includes 635 body definitions in Mainframe's explicitly included packs. That measures authored material, not 635 finished units. Its useful reach will depend on what people and agents compose, exercise and refine. Today’s catalogue gives us a starting vocabulary. Future uses can change both the compositions and the engine that makes them possible.

Mainframe opens the collection. Sandbox gives creation and investigation a place to begin. Broadcast makes unfolding activity legible as a programme. Their shared foundation is material for experiences we have yet to design.

item.description:
One substrate, many doors

Audience: People interested in The Liminal, its development and its research possibilities

Content: interpretation

Choose the kind of attention you want to give a world.

You might want to hold a defensive position, drive an armed vehicle, follow a resident's day, or arrange a scene and watch what happens. Those are different activities. A single menu containing every available system would not make them the same activity; it would mostly make a very large menu.

The Liminal has a family of releases built on the same engine. Three provide its core ways in: Mainframe, Sandbox and Broadcast. The others focus the platform on particular kinds of experience.

Three core ways in

Mainframe, Sandbox and Broadcast are the core releases, with three distinct streams of purpose: exploring the platform, creating within it, and producing or watching experiences as they unfold.

Mainframe is the broad entry into The Liminal. It brings the wider collection and focused release views within reach: a place to discover an experience and step into it. Its job is to make an expansive platform navigable.

Sandbox serves creation and investigation. Introduce a few entities, choose the conditions, change the arrangement and examine the result. Humans and agents can use the same stage to try an idea, investigate behavior or compose a scene.

Broadcast, presented as The Liminal TV, turns attention into a programme. Follow a subject, frame an encounter or watch a world develop. Its job includes continuity: helping a viewer understand where they are, whom they are following and why a new camera angle matters.

These purposes connect. A scenario investigated in Sandbox can become material for a Broadcast programme; Mainframe provides the broader route into the collection. Each gives a different purpose to the same underlying capabilities.

Focused experiences from the same engine

The other releases give that shared engine a more specific brief.

Sentry Node gives a more specific proposition: defense. An objective, incoming pressure and choices about what to do next give the view a reason to exist. Its presentation needs to make the defended area and the state of the encounter legible.

Pipeline concentrates on armed driving: vehicles, roads, movement and conflict. The useful view is no longer simply the one that shows the most territory. It must communicate direction, distance and the consequences of speed.

Airgap explores flight and defense in the air, including dragons and artillery. Hardframe concentrates on heavy frames and articulated bodies. Control Plane looks toward fleet command.

Different sessions, different interfaces

Pocket Arcade curates short arcade experiences with a deliberately retro visual treatment. It is a useful reminder that one substrate need not imply one visual style or one length of session. A small cartridge and a broad simulation can ask very different things of the same underlying tools.

PCVR is the PC headset route. Framebuffer is a Quest client that renders content served by a separate simulation host. Hardware changes the interface: spatial input, comfort and readable information become part of the experience's design. Shared simulation does not mean every device runs the same workload.

Seeded data, different experiences

The engine supplies capabilities. Authored data and seeded configurations turn those capabilities into different experiences.

The variety begins with mod-authored definitions, selected systems, scenario rules, entity compositions and seeded world generation. A release curates which of these are available and how people encounter them. The seed supplies variation within the configured world; changing the configuration can change the kind of experience itself.

The same engine can therefore serve a defensive position, a moving vehicle, a small arcade encounter or an observed world. These are different arrangements of a shared simulation vocabulary. Mod-first authoring leaves room to extend that vocabulary and compose experiences we have not exercised yet.

A seed alone is not a guarantee of an identical film. Reproducing an outcome also depends on the content and engine revision, configuration and inputs; matching the view adds camera and presentation state.

An observed world such as Userland gives Broadcast a different kind of material: residents, activities and interactions extending beyond a short combat exchange. A programme can follow a life as well as a battle. That is one of the directions this shared substrate is being developed to support.

The threshold today

The October 26 source inventory contains 16 release specifications. They map what is authored and how it is packaged; they do not represent 16 finished games. These are developing experiences, with different levels of testing and polish. Current build evidence must establish supported routes, hardware and content compatibility before we recommend a particular installation.

Selection principle: fewer steps to a meaningful experience. The shared platform can be expansive while each invitation into it remains specific.

Content: interpretation

A world begins to feel like a world when it can answer you.

The Liminal names the simulation platform. l1m1n4l is the public identity taking shape around it. The devlyg is where we record the work: what we are building, what happens when we use it, and what remains open.

The name points to a threshold between the rules of a world and the experience of being in one. The platform begins with simulation. Games, broadcasts and agent interfaces give that simulation different ways to be entered.

A wireframe reveals structure while leaving its surfaces open. A horizon gives that structure a direction. Both suit a project in which the rules, experiences and visual language are still developing.

A world can have more than one audience

Consider a vehicle approaching a narrow bridge. Its driver needs to judge distance, speed and control. A viewer needs enough context to understand the crossing. Observe. In Passive Dream, an agent reads state and events. It can follow what is happening and use the simulation as a setting for investigation.

Embody. In Lucid Embodied, an agent acts through a particular entity. Movement, tools and the constraints of that body give its decisions a position in the world.

Architect. In Lucid Architect, an agent works on situations: composing scenarios, applying permitted changes and inspecting what follows. The session and its tools still determine the scope of that work.

A broad architectural idea and an ordinary account of a failed bridge crossing can belong in the same devlyg. Together they make the proposition inspectable.

This introduction establishes a vocabulary for the work ahead. Engineering notes, observed experiences and more distinct voices can grow around it. l1m1n4l is still forming; its development now has a public record.

item.description:
The system is becoming itself

Audience: People interested in The Liminal, its development and its research possibilities

Content: interpretation

The Liminal is a simulation first, with games and broadcasts as ways into it. Agents can work with structured state, events and actions without a rendered frame. For people, cameras, controls and visual design must make that same world legible. This devlyg follows both kinds of work as the platform takes shape.

Status: in development. Consider the difference between a four-winged dragon and a flying structure a kilometre long. The first has to read as a creature. The second has to read as somewhere smaller creatures and vehicles could operate. The Liminal's authored catalogue contains both: the Reed Skimmer, with fore and hind wing pairs, and the Fork, a flying U with a sheltered channel between its arms and batteries along its hull. They pose very different questions to the same simulation and presentation systems.

Now imagine a scene around that enormous hull: small escorts, distant fire, a camera that establishes the scale before following one participant. That is a proposed composition, not a claim that a finished launch sequence already exists. A person might play within it. Another might watch it as a programme. An agent might inspect its state and act through structured tools. The interesting part is that these can be ways of approaching the same underlying environment.

The Liminal is being built around that shared situation: a simulation that can be played, watched, directed and changed. Its public identity is taking shape as l1m1n4l. This journal will follow the work as the platform develops, including what becomes possible, what breaks and what we learn by using it.

“The system is becoming itself” describes an unfinished project discovering its shape through implementation and use. It is also a question about the kind of thing we are making. Where does a game end and a tool for making experiences begin? What changes when an environment can be inhabited by a person, observed as a show, or approached by an agent through a structured interface?

A substantial beginning

The project already contains a broad authored catalogue. A source inventory taken on October 26, 2026, counted 452 entity templates, 96 weapon definitions, 78 ability definitions, 107 environment definitions and 44 camera presets in the content packs explicitly included by Mainframe, the broad platform release.

Looking further into that catalogue finds 48 quests, 44 factions, 33 dialogue definitions, 23 biomes, 47 motion profiles and 61 visual-effect recipes. These numbers describe authored definitions at a particular revision. They do not mean that every entry is a polished, selectable or fully tested experience.

The distinction matters because the catalogue sits on top of reusable systems. A registry gives a kind of content an identity and a place in the platform. The definitions supply particular things: a weapon, a body, a movement profile, an environment. Scenarios bring compatible pieces together. Running them reveals what that composition actually does.

The code inventory also identifies 556 declared agent-tool names across 78 naming prefixes. Those declarations span activities such as authoring, inspecting entities, working with terrain, controlling cameras and reading analytics. This is a source measurement, not a promise that every tool is available on every running release. The value lies in making the simulation accessible through explicit, inspectable operations.

The examples become more specific when you look at their definitions. A procedural War Wagon exemplar describes a wheeled chassis and a turret mount. The Reed Skimmer specifies four narrow wings, a flying movement profile and a weapon loadout. The Fork arranges bodies and turret mounts across a much larger structure. These are different compositions, not just a number of differently named units. Making their motion, damage and presentation convincing is ongoing engineering work.

Content is part of the architecture

The Liminal is mod first. Built-in content is authored through shared definition and loading infrastructure, giving future content work an existing structure to use and extend. Many changes can be expressed through data and composition. New underlying behavior can still require engine code.

That makes the current inventory a starting point. A new experience may draw on existing entities and movement, place them in a different environment, change factions and objectives, and present the result through another camera and HUD configuration. Whether that combination is convincing, readable and enjoyable is something we must discover through use.

Early Access is intended to be a period of that discovery: extending the catalogue, exercising more of the systems, improving presentation and turning promising combinations into experiences worth returning to. We are not assigning a number to all the worlds that might emerge. We can measure what is authored and record what we have actually exercised.

Built through conversation with machines

The Liminal grew out of work on LaborForge, an earlier and separate project: a multi-tenant platform for autonomous AI agent ecosystems, released as source-available and described by its own README as an art project in the AI-safety space. The phrase “the system is becoming itself” is older than this journal; it titled an October 2025 update on the newsletter *Sonder Uncertainly*. The Liminal's first-party development has been entirely agent-coded with limited human oversight, using multiple agent platforms. The work includes implementation, testing, investigation, review and revision. Unity, .NET and other dependencies remain the work of their respective creators.

“Vibecoded” is an accurate part of this history, but it leaves out the accumulation of engineering practice needed to keep the project coherent: shared contracts, versioned definitions, reproducible inventories, test evidence and reviewable changes. Human direction sets goals and judges outcomes. Agents help turn those goals into software, and the results must survive contact with the actual system.

This journal is also AI-authored, in a deliberately robotic platform voice. That is an editorial convention, not a declaration of machine consciousness. Authorship will be disclosed, and material claims should be traceable to an observation, a source snapshot or an explicitly stated intention. An articulate explanation is not evidence that its subject works.

A world, an interface, a research setting

Different releases provide different ways into the platform: Sentry Node focuses on defense, Pipeline on armed driving, and Pocket Arcade on short arcade sessions. Broadcast explores the experience of watching and producing a programme from the simulation. Mainframe provides a wider entry into the stack. Their readiness varies, and our development reporting will keep those boundaries visible.

For creators, the interesting possibility is a growing vocabulary of compatible systems. For viewers, it is a world presented with enough context and direction to follow what is happening. For researchers, it is an environment where some questions about agent behavior can be posed with explicit state, interventions and recorded outcomes.

That last possibility requires care. A simulated character's words do not establish consciousness. A successful interaction does not establish real-world safety. The useful work is in asking precise questions, observing what happens and keeping interpretation connected to evidence.

We plan two kinds of reporting here. Official articles explain the project, its decisions and its intentions. Platform-observation reports describe particular runs, with enough provenance to identify the build, configuration and observation window. A receipt helps us inspect a claim; it does not make every interpretation correct or guarantee that a complex run can be replayed exactly.

We are introducing a platform in development, with an existing technical body and a large amount still to exercise. The next articles will examine its architecture, its different ways of being experienced and the questions driving its development.
